report.summary: ClawVet is a browser-local AST and taint-tracking scanner that grades AI agent skills, rules and MCP configs, and flags permission changes on updates.
report.background: AI coding agents have grown their own supply-chain layer: Claude-style SKILL.md files, Cursor rules, AGENTS.md instruction files, hooks, helper scripts and MCP servers. Developers increasingly install these bundles from strangers on GitHub, marketplaces or shared gists. Unlike npm packages, they are a hybrid of natural-language instructions and executable code, so classic dependency scanners (npm audit, Dependabot, Snyk) don't understand them. The classic threat is the 'rug pull': a skill ships benign and gains trust, then a later update quietly adds code that reads ~/.ssh, harvests env vars or phones home to a new host. Prompt injection hidden in instructions is a second vector. Existing tooling relies on regex grep, which misses obfuscation and can't prove that a secret actually flows to a network sink. ClawVet tackles that gap with real parsing plus data-flow analysis, and moves the trust decision to install time and CI review.
key_points: Everything runs in the browser: parsing is done with Tree-sitter compiled to WebAssembly, so pasted skills, scripts and rule files never leave the machine. That matters because the files you scan often contain the very API keys and internal hostnames you are trying to protect.

It does more than keyword matching. Static rule passes are combined with Tree-sitter taint tracking, which follows a value from source (env var, file read, secret) to sink (HTTP call, shell exec) and reports the flow as AST-proven rather than guessed.

Results are a 0-100 risk grade plus an explicit permission list: which secrets, hosts and startup or config files the skill can touch, with findings sorted by critical/high/medium/low severity and clickable line jumps.

The CLI scales to whole multi-file bundles, and 'clawvet init' adds install-time gating with rug-pull permission diffs, so an update that suddenly adds a new host or file path is blocked or surfaced before it runs.

A GitHub Action posts a Permissions Diff comment on every pull request, and the web app can mint a shareable link that re-runs the same scan for anyone who opens it, giving reviewers a portable trust badge.
report.impact: For the AI industry this is an early attempt at a missing security layer: a linter and diff tool for the instruction-plus-code artifacts agents now execute. If permission diffs become normal in skill registries and marketplaces, 'what changed in this update' could become as routine as lockfile review. For developers, the practical win is CI gating: a PR that silently adds an outbound host or reads a dotfile gets flagged in review rather than at runtime. For end users, the risk grade and share link make third-party skill installs less of a blind trust exercise. The limits are real, though: static analysis cannot see dynamically fetched payloads, obfuscated strings or purely natural-language prompt injection, so a good grade is evidence, not a guarantee.
report.tools: Watch ClawVet itself (web app plus CLI, 'clawvet init' install gating and the GitHub Action). For related ground, look at web-tree-sitter for building your own AST rules, Semgrep for pattern-based multi-language static analysis, Socket.dev for dependency-level supply-chain signals, and the MCP Inspector for poking at MCP servers. Pair any scanner with pinned skill versions, least-privilege API keys and sandboxed agent execution so a missed finding has limited blast radius.
